lessons.title: streamline
lessons.meaning: To make a process more efficient by removing unnecessary steps or complexity.
lessons.example: We streamlined the approval process by replacing three separate forms with one.
lessons.notes: Streamline takes an object: streamline a workflow, service, or procedure. It emphasizes how something operates, rather than simply doing it faster. Simplify is broader; an explanation can be simplified without being streamlined. Avoid claiming efficiency if you have only moved work onto someone else.
lessons.conversation:
A: These requests pass through four different teams.
B: Could we streamline the approval process?
A: We could remove the duplicate review.
B: That would save time without skipping the necessary checks.
lessons.exercise: Improve this proposal using streamline: We should remove duplicate forms and unnecessary approvals. Model: We should streamline the process by removing duplicate forms and unnecessary approvals.

scene.description: A professional pointing at a clipboard with an overly complex diagram, focused on making it simpler.

lessons.title: grasp
lessons.meaning: To understand an idea, especially one that initially seems difficult or unfamiliar.
lessons.example: I grasp the basic argument, but I am not convinced by the evidence.
lessons.notes: Grasp an idea, principle, implication, or concept. Understanding an argument does not mean agreeing with it. I cannot quite grasp it sounds less absolute than I do not understand anything. The noun a grasp of describes understanding: She has a solid grasp of the subject.
lessons.conversation:
A: Do you grasp how the new system works?
B: I grasp the principle, but the setup still confuses me.
A: Shall we work through one example?
B: Yes, that would help me connect the steps.
lessons.exercise: Distinguish understanding from agreement. Model: I grasp your argument, although I disagree with your conclusion. Then write one sentence using a solid grasp of.

scene.description: A person standing in a warm-lit room, looking up at a glowing lightbulb with a smile.

lessons.title: trade off
lessons.meaning: To accept less of one desirable outcome in exchange for more of another.
lessons.example: We are trading off convenience against privacy when we keep every account signed in.
lessons.notes: Trade off X against Y makes the competing priorities explicit. In American English, trade X for Y is also natural, but may describe a simple exchange. The noun is a trade-off, with a hyphen; the verb is trade off. Specify the cost rather than using trade off as a vague synonym for decide.
lessons.conversation:
A: Could we make the app easier to access?
B: Yes, but we would be trading off security against convenience.
A: Is there a way to reduce that cost?
B: We could keep a quick login while requiring checks for sensitive actions.
lessons.exercise: Turn the noun into a verb: There is a trade-off between speed and accuracy. Model: We are trading off accuracy against speed. Explain which outcome your wording prioritizes.

scene.description: A person looking at a balance scale with weights on each side, showing a difficult choice.

lessons.title: zero in on
lessons.meaning: To focus increasingly closely on a specific issue, detail, or likely explanation.
lessons.example: After reviewing the complaints, we zeroed in on the confusing checkout instructions.
lessons.notes: Zero in on suggests narrowing attention from several possibilities to one target. It does not imply that you have proved the explanation correct. Say zero in on the cause, rather than zero on the cause. It works in conversations about investigations, planning, and problem-solving; it can sound overly aggressive when directed at a person.
lessons.conversation:
A: Have you figured out why customers are leaving?
B: We have zeroed in on the checkout process.
A: Do we know which step is causing trouble?
B: Not yet. We are testing the delivery options first.
lessons.exercise: Show narrowed attention without overstating certainty. Model: We have zeroed in on the payment screen as a possible source of confusion, but we still need to test it.

scene.description: A person standing in the middle of a road fork, holding a map and deciding which way to go.

lessons.title: damn with faint praise
lessons.meaning: To weaken someone or something with praise so restrained that it implies a negative judgment.
lessons.example: Calling her excellent presentation adequate damned it with faint praise.
lessons.notes: The phrase describes an inferred attitude, not a literal insult. Adequate can be neutral when basic sufficiency is the real criterion; it becomes faint praise when excellence is expected or deserved. Consider context, tone, and comparison before inferring hostility. This expression is more common in commentary than in friendly small talk.
lessons.conversation:
A: The review said the performance was competent.
B: That sounds positive at first.
A: But the reviewer called every other performer outstanding.
B: In that context, competent rather damns her with faint praise.
lessons.exercise: Explain the implication of The meal was edible in an enthusiastic restaurant review. Model: It suggests mere acceptability rather than enjoyment; the low standard makes the apparent praise sound critical.

scene.description: A proud presenter points to a rising chart while a listener gives a restrained skeptical shrug, making faint praise visibly less enthusiastic than the achievement deserves.

lessons.title: under the gun
lessons.meaning: Under strong pressure, usually because a deadline is close.
lessons.example: We are under the gun to finish the proposal before the client meeting.
lessons.notes: This is an informal American expression. It emphasizes pressure, not literal danger. Under pressure is more suitable for a formal report or a sensitive conversation. Use under the gun to do something; avoid under a gun. Be specific about the deadline so the listener understands what help you need.
lessons.conversation:
A: Can you review these slides today?
B: I can, but I am under the gun with another deadline.
A: Would tomorrow morning be more realistic?
B: Yes. Send them over and I will review them before lunch.
lessons.exercise: Make this request considerate: We are under the gun, so help us now. Model: We are under the gun to finish by Friday. Would you have time to review one section today?

scene.description: A person looking anxiously at a clock on the wall while holding an important envelope.

lessons.title: Let's leave some room for flexibility.
lessons.meaning: A collaborative way to suggest keeping a plan open to reasonable changes.
lessons.example: We have a useful outline, but let us leave some room for flexibility if the weather changes.
lessons.notes: Leave room for is a natural expression meaning allow space or possibility. Flexibility concerns adaptation; vagueness concerns missing detail. This phrase works best after agreeing on the essentials. Otherwise, it may sound like avoiding a commitment. The contraction let us becomes let's in ordinary speech and writing.
lessons.conversation:
A: Shall we schedule every stop before the trip?
B: Let us book the essentials and leave some room for flexibility.
A: What should we decide now?
B: The hotel and transport. We can choose the afternoon activities later.
lessons.exercise: Suggest a flexible plan with one clear commitment. Model: Let us confirm dinner for six and leave some room for flexibility about what we do afterward.

scene.description: A planner keeps a timetable open while leaving another route available, illustrating flexibility rather than a rigid plan.

lessons.title: Were it not for: present hypothetical inversion
lessons.meaning: Were it not for introduces a hypothetical situation in which a current condition is absent.
lessons.example: Were it not for the grant, the research team would have to close the project.
lessons.notes: This formal construction means If it were not for; omit if and place were before it. It normally introduces an imagined change to a current situation. To describe a past counterfactual, use Had it not been for the grant, the team would have closed. Choose the form according to the time of the imagined situation, rather than simply when the grant arrived.
lessons.conversation:
A: Why does the report mention the grant so prominently?
B: Were it not for that support, the project would be impossible.
A: Are you describing the current situation?
B: Exactly. For last year, I would use Had it not been for.
lessons.exercise: Rewrite for a past consequence: If it had not been for her help, we would have missed the deadline. Model: Had it not been for her help, we would have missed the deadline.

scene.description: A grant envelope supports a bridge carrying a research book; without that support the project cannot move ahead, illustrating a current hypothetical dependency.

lessons.title: Give your next step more attention than your last stumble.
lessons.meaning: Focus on a useful action after a setback instead of dwelling on the mistake.
lessons.example: After a difficult presentation, her colleague said, “Give your next step more attention than your last stumble.” She decided to rehearse the opening again.
lessons.notes: Stumble is a metaphor for a minor mistake; next step means the next action. Use the line to redirect attention after acknowledging the problem, not to dismiss its consequences.
lessons.conversation:
A: I cannot stop thinking about my mistake.
B: “Give your next step more attention than your last stumble.” What could you change?
A: I could check the figures before presenting.
B: Good. That addresses the problem directly.
lessons.exercise: Use the quote after acknowledging a setback, then suggest a concrete action. Model: The error mattered. Now check the figures and send a correction.

scene.description: A person moves from a worried glance at a question mark to a checked practical next step on a clipboard.

lessons.title: Any plans you are looking forward to?
lessons.meaning: An open-ended, low-pressure question that invites someone to share an upcoming activity.
lessons.example: Any plans you are looking forward to this weekend, or are you keeping it low-key?
lessons.notes: Looking forward to takes a noun or an -ing form. Keeping it low-key means choosing something relaxed. Offer an easy alternative so the question does not imply that exciting plans are expected. Follow the detail your partner shares instead of switching straight to your own story.
lessons.conversation:
A: Any plans you are looking forward to this weekend?
B: A short hike, if the weather holds.
A: Nice. Have you picked a trail yet?
B: A quiet one near the lake. What about you?
A: I am keeping it low-key, probably reading at home.
B: That sounds lovely. Anything good on your reading list?
A: A mystery novel I have been saving for a quiet afternoon.
B: Enjoy it. We can compare weekend highlights on Monday.
lessons.exercise: Respond with a plan, one detail, and a question back. Model: I am meeting a friend for coffee near the park. Are you doing anything outdoors?

scene.description: Two colleagues standing near a coffee station, talking and smiling.

lessons.title: Planning flexibly under pressure
lessons.meaning: A short model essay brings today’s language together in one situation.
paragraphs: Good planning balances clear priorities with room to adapt.
Our team was under the gun to organize a weekend event.
We needed to streamline the booking process and grasp the practical constraints.
After we zeroed in on the main problem, we discussed what we would trade off: convenience or privacy.
“Let’s leave some room for flexibility,” I suggested.
Were it not for our backup plan, a change in the weather would force us to cancel.
When a friend asked about plans I was looking forward to, I explained how we had prepared for uncertainty.
We can prepare carefully without expecting every detail to go perfectly.
lessons.structure: Introduction → reason and example → another angle or reflection → conclusion. Use 1–2 / 2–3 / 2–3 / 1–2 sentences.
lessons.exercise: Your turn: Write four short paragraphs about a similar choice. Reuse two expressions and today’s grammar.
lessons.example:
Good planning balances clear priorities with room to adapt.

Our team was under the gun to organize a weekend event. We needed to streamline the booking process and grasp the practical constraints. After we zeroed in on the main problem, we discussed what we would trade off: convenience or privacy.

“Let’s leave some room for flexibility,” I suggested. Were it not for our backup plan, a change in the weather would force us to cancel. When a friend asked about plans I was looking forward to, I explained how we had prepared for uncertainty.

We can prepare carefully without expecting every detail to go perfectly.
lessons.notes: Notice how each paragraph develops the same central idea.

recipes.title: Smoky Black Bean and Corn Stuffed Peppers
steps: Cook brown rice with the measured water according to the package directions. Preheat the oven to 375°F / 190°C and halve peppers lengthwise, removing seeds.
Heat oil in a wide pan. Soften onion for 5 minutes, then stir in paprika, cumin, tomatoes and salt; simmer for 5 minutes.
Fold in the drained cooked beans, corn and cooked rice. Stir until the filling is hot throughout, adding no uncooked beans.
Arrange twelve pepper halves in two baking dishes. Divide filling evenly among them and cover the dishes loosely with foil.
Bake for 30 minutes. Remove foil, scatter cheese evenly and bake for another 10 minutes, until peppers are tender and filling reaches 165°F / 74°C.
Serve two pepper halves per person. Cool leftovers in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.
recipes.allergens: Milk; check canned products for additional allergens

recipes.title: Cinnamon Peanut Butter Oat Bites
steps: Check that the peanut butter contains no unexpected allergens. Combine oats, chopped raisins, chia seeds and cinnamon in a large bowl.
Stir peanut butter, honey and measured water together in a separate bowl until evenly blended; use room-temperature peanut butter to make mixing easier.
Add the wet mixture to the dry ingredients. Fold thoroughly until every patch of oats is moistened and the mixture holds together when squeezed.
Refrigerate the bowl for 20 minutes to let the oats and chia absorb moisture. Divide the mixture into eighteen equal portions.
Roll each portion into a compact ball with clean hands and arrange in a single layer in a covered container.
Serve three bites per person. Keep refrigerated and consume within 3 days; do not store these moist bites at room temperature.
recipes.allergens: Peanuts; oats may contain wheat unless certified gluten-free

recipes.title: Caramelized Onion and White Bean Skillet
steps: Heat olive oil in a wide heavy pan over medium-low heat. Add onions and cook for 20 minutes, stirring frequently, until soft and golden rather than scorched.
Add diced carrots and garlic. Cook for 5 minutes while stirring, then add thyme, stock and the drained, fully cooked beans.
Bring to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for 10 minutes until the carrots are tender and the sauce lightly thickens.
Fold in spinach in two batches, allowing it to wilt. Add lemon juice, salt and pepper; taste before adding any additional seasoning.
Toast the measured bread in a dry skillet or toaster. Divide the beans and vegetables among six shallow bowls and serve each with 60g bread.
Refrigerate the bean mixture within 2 hours; store bread separately so it keeps its texture.
recipes.allergens: Wheat in bread; stock may contain celery or other allergens

recipes.title: Apple and Raisin Hand Pies
steps: Preheat the oven to 400°F / 200°C. Put apples, raisins, sugar, lemon juice and cinnamon in a saucepan with 30mL water.
Simmer for 5 minutes. Mix cornstarch with the remaining water, stir into the fruit and cook for 1 minute until thickened. Spread filling on a plate and cool completely.
Keep pastry cold while cutting twelve equal rectangles. Spoon cooled filling onto six rectangles, leaving a clear 1cm border around the edges.
Cover each with another rectangle. Press edges firmly with a fork, cut two small steam vents in each top and transfer to a lined tray.
Brush with beaten egg. Bake for 20-25 minutes until deeply golden, with cooked pastry at the base and no wet egg glaze.
Cool for 10 minutes before serving one pie per person. Refrigerate any leftover pies within 2 hours.
recipes.allergens: Wheat, egg; pastry may contain milk or soy

recipes.title: Miso-Glazed Shiitake and Tofu Donburi

ingredients.name: Water mixed with rice vinegar (45mL water + 15mL rice vinegar)

steps: Rinse rice until water runs clear and cook in a rice cooker or covered pot using the 750mL water.
Whisk miso, the measured water-vinegar mixture, soy sauce, and sugar in a small bowl until smooth to create the glaze.
Heat 15mL oil in a large non-stick skillet over medium-high heat. Brown the tofu cubes on all sides for about 6-8 minutes, then remove them from the pan.
Add the remaining 15mL oil to the same pan and sauté the shiitake mushrooms for 5 minutes until softened and fragrant.
Return the tofu to the pan with the mushrooms. Pour the miso glaze over the mixture and stir gently for 3-4 minutes until the sauce bubbles and coats the ingredients evenly.
Ensure the internal temperature of the tofu reaches 160°F / 71°C.
Divide the cooked rice into six deep bowls. Spoon the miso tofu and mushroom mixture generously over the rice.
Garnish with sliced scallions and serve immediately.
recipes.allergens: Soy, wheat in soy sauce; check miso label
recipes.note: Refrigerate any leftovers within 2 hours of cooking. Use within 3-4 days and reheat until steaming hot (165°F / 74°C). Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.

recipes.title: Nori-Crusted Crispy Rice Crackers
steps: Preheat the oven to 400°F / 200°C and line a large baking sheet with parchment paper.
In a bowl, mix cold rice with shredded nori, soy sauce, sesame oil, and cornstarch until the rice is sticky and well-coated.
Spread the mixture onto the parchment paper in a very thin, even layer about 0.5cm thick.
Bake for 20-25 minutes, checking frequently, until the edges are golden brown and the center is completely crisp.
Remove from the oven and while still warm, sprinkle immediately with sesame seeds.
Let the sheet cool completely on the tray, as it will continue to harden and become crunchy.
Break the large sheet into smaller, irregular snack-sized shards.
Divide into six portions and serve.
recipes.allergens: Soy, sesame, wheat in soy sauce
recipes.note: Best enjoyed fresh for maximum crispness. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish. Use cold rice that was refrigerated within 2 hours after cooking; do not use rice left at room temperature overnight.
recipes.storage: Use promptly. Refrigerate within 2 hours, use within 3 days and reheat to 165°F / 74°C; rice snacks are not assumed shelf-stable.

recipes.title: Lemon-Garlic White Fish with Roasted Fennel
steps: Preheat the oven to 400°F / 200°C. Put couscous in a heatproof bowl, add the measured boiling water, cover for 5 minutes and fluff with a fork.
Place the fennel wedges and cherry tomatoes on a large rimmed baking sheet. Drizzle with 30mL of olive oil, sprinkle with half the salt and pepper, and toss to coat.
Roast the vegetables for 15 minutes until they begin to soften.
In a small bowl, whisk the remaining 30mL olive oil, garlic, lemon juice, and oregano.
Pat the fish dry and place the fillets on top of the vegetables. Brush the fish generously with the lemon-garlic mixture.
Return to the oven and roast for 10-12 minutes, or until the fish reaches an internal temperature of 145°F / 63°C and flakes easily with a fork.
Divide the couscous, roasted vegetables and fish among six plates.
Drizzle any remaining pan juices over the fish before serving.
recipes.note: Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Use within 3 days. Reheat to 165°F / 74°C. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate fish and couscous within 2 hours; use within 3 days. Reheat to 165°F / 74°C.

recipes.title: Marinated Olive and Artichoke Medley

ingredients.name: Canned artichoke hearts, drained and halved

steps: Drain the artichoke hearts well and pat dry to ensure the marinade sticks.
In a medium bowl, combine the olives and artichoke hearts.
Add the olive oil, lemon zest, fresh rosemary, sliced garlic, and red pepper flakes.
Toss everything together until the ingredients are thoroughly coated in the oil and herbs.
Cover the bowl and let the mixture sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes to allow the flavors to meld.
If preparing ahead, refrigerate for up to 24 hours and bring to room temperature before serving.
Divide into six small bowls for serving.
Serve with toothpicks for easy snacking.
recipes.note: This snack is best when allowed to marinate for at least 30 minutes. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Store in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

recipes.title: Autumn Mushroom and Ginger Braised Chicken
steps: Rinse the measured rice and cook with 600mL rice water according to package instructions.
Heat oil in a large wok or heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat. Add ginger and garlic, stir-frying for 1 minute until highly aromatic.
Add chicken pieces to the pan. Sear for 5-6 minutes until lightly browned on all sides.
Add sliced mushrooms and cook for 3 minutes until softened. Stir in the sugar, soy sauce, and dark soy sauce, coating the chicken evenly.
Pour in the water and bring to a gentle boil. Reduce heat to low, cover with a lid, and simmer for 20-25 minutes.
Remove the lid and increase the heat to medium-high for 5 minutes, stirring frequently to reduce the sauce until it becomes thick and glossy.
Check that chicken reaches 165°F / 74°C. Remove from heat and stir in half the scallions.
Divide rice into six bowls, top with the chicken and mushroom mixture, and garnish with remaining scallions.
recipes.note: Use fresh shiitake if available for a deeper autumn flavor profile. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container within 2 hours. Consume within 3-4 days. Reheat to 165°F / 74°C.

recipes.title: Crispy Five-Spice Tofu Bites

ingredients.name: Extra firm tofu, pressed and 2cm cubes

steps: Pat pressed tofu cubes extremely dry with a clean kitchen towel to ensure crispiness.
In a shallow bowl, toss tofu cubes with cornstarch until every side is evenly coated; shake off excess.
Heat oil in a deep pan to 350°F / 175°C. Test temperature with a small piece of tofu; it should sizzle immediately.
Fry the tofu in three batches to avoid overcrowding the pan, cooking for 5-6 minutes per batch until golden and crispy.
Remove tofu using a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack for 2 minutes.
In a small bowl, whisk together the five-spice powder, salt, and white pepper.
While the tofu is still hot, sprinkle the seasoning mixture over the bites and toss gently.
Divide into six small bowls and serve immediately while hot and crunchy.
recipes.note: Pressing the tofu for at least 30 minutes before cutting is essential for texture. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours; use within 3 days. Reheat to 165°F / 74°C before serving.

recipes.title: Taiwanese Braised Pork Rice Bowls
steps: Cook the 450g rice with 600mL rice water according to package instructions.
In a heavy-bottomed pot, brown the ground pork over medium heat until it reaches 160°F / 71°C. Remove pork and set aside.
In the same pot, fry shallots and garlic in the rendered pork fat until golden brown.
Return pork to the pot. Stir in the rock sugar, soy sauce, deglazing water, and five-spice powder.
Pour in water, bring to a simmer, and cook covered on low heat for 45 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Remove the lid and simmer for another 10-15 minutes until the sauce is thick and flavorful.
While the meat finishes, steam the bok choy until tender.
Divide rice into six bowls, top with the braised pork mixture, and serve with a side of steamed bok choy.
recipes.note: The key to this dish is the slow reduction of the sauce to develop a deep, savory flavor. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container within 2 hours. Consume within 3-4 days. Reheat to 165°F / 74°C.

recipes.title: Sweet Potato and Scallion Fritters
steps: In a large bowl, combine the shredded sweet potato, scallions, flour, cornstarch, and salt.
Gradually stir in the water until a thick, cohesive batter forms; the mixture should bind the potatoes together.
Heat 20mL of oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium heat.
Scoop 1/6 of the batter into the pan for each fritter, flattening with a spatula to about 10cm diameter.
Cook for 5-6 minutes per side until the sweet potato is tender and the edges are deeply golden and crispy.
Remove from the pan and drain on paper towels to remove excess oil.
Repeat for all six fritters, adding remaining oil as necessary.
Serve warm, cut into wedges if desired.
recipes.note: Ensure the sweet potato is shredded finely so it cooks through quickly. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours; consume within 3 days. Reheat in a 350°F / 175°C oven for 8-10 minutes to restore crispness.

recipes.title: Tomato and Egg Noodle Bowls
steps: Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Cook noodles according to package directions, adding bok choy for the last 2 minutes, then drain well.
Beat eggs with salt. Heat 30mL oil in a wide nonstick pan and scramble the eggs gently until fully set; transfer to a clean bowl.
Add remaining oil and tomato wedges to the pan. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until tomatoes begin releasing juice.
Stir in soy sauce, sugar and the measured sauce water. Simmer for 3 minutes, then return cooked eggs and fold gently into the tomatoes.
Heat the combined egg mixture to 160°F / 71°C. Divide noodles and bok choy among six bowls and spoon the tomato-egg sauce over them.
Scatter scallions across the bowls. Serve immediately and refrigerate leftovers in shallow containers within 2 hours.
recipes.note: Photo illustrates a similar dish; appearance and ingredients may differ. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate in shallow covered containers within 2 hours; use within 3 days. Reheat cooked leftovers to 165°F / 74°C.

recipes.title: Sesame Coconut Pudding Squares
steps: Line a 20cm square shallow container with parchment paper, leaving edges overhanging so the set pudding can be lifted out safely.
Whisk cornstarch with 150mL of the cold milk in a small bowl until no lumps remain. Combine remaining milk, coconut milk and sugar in a saucepan.
Warm the saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring until sugar dissolves. Pour in the cornstarch mixture slowly while whisking continuously.
Cook gently for 3-5 minutes until the pudding thickens and bubbles. Keep stirring to prevent sticking, then fold in the toasted sesame seeds.
Pour into the lined container and smooth the top. Cool briefly, refrigerate within 2 hours and chill for at least 4 hours until firm.
Lift out, cut eighteen squares and coat lightly with shredded coconut. Serve three squares per person and keep all remaining pudding refrigerated.
recipes.note: Photo illustrates a similar dish; appearance and ingredients may differ. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish. Allow at least 4 hours of chilling beyond preparation and cooking.
recipes.storage: Keep covered and refrigerated; consume within 3 days. Serve chilled. Additional chilling time: at least 4 hours.

recipes.title: Soy Garlic Chicken and Cabbage Rice Bowls

ingredients.name: Boneless chicken thighs, cut into 3cm pieces

steps: Cook rice with the measured rice water according to the package instructions. Mix soy sauce, garlic, ginger, sugar and sauce water in a bowl.
Heat oil in a wide deep skillet over medium-high heat. Add chicken in two batches and brown for 4 minutes per batch, then return all chicken to the pan.
Add cabbage and carrots. Stir for 3 minutes to begin softening the vegetables, then pour the soy-garlic mixture over everything.
Reduce heat, cover and simmer for 10-15 minutes, stirring occasionally. Check several chicken pieces with a food thermometer; each must reach 165°F / 74°C.
Remove the lid and simmer briefly if the sauce is too thin. Divide rice among six bowls and add equal portions of chicken and vegetables.
Garnish with scallions and sesame seeds. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and reheat to 165°F / 74°C.
recipes.allergens: Soy, wheat in soy sauce, sesame
recipes.note: Photo illustrates a similar dish; appearance and ingredients may differ. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate in shallow covered containers within 2 hours; use within 3 days. Reheat cooked leftovers to 165°F / 74°C.

recipes.title: Crunchy Seaweed and Rice Puff Clusters
steps: Preheat the oven to 300°F / 150°C. Line a large shallow tray with baking parchment and measure the cereal into a heatproof mixing bowl.
Cut toasted nori into very small pieces using clean kitchen scissors. Toss through the cereal with the toasted sesame seeds so the dry mixture is evenly distributed.
Warm brown rice syrup, soy sauce and oil in a small saucepan over low heat for 1 minute, just until easy to stir; do not boil vigorously.
Pour the warm syrup over the cereal and immediately fold with a spatula until coated. Spread thinly on the lined tray without packing it into a thick slab.
Bake for 15 minutes, stirring once halfway through. Let cool completely on the tray so the mixture firms into crisp clusters.
Break into eighteen small clusters and divide three per person. Store only fully dry, crisp clusters in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days.
recipes.allergens: Sesame, soy, wheat in soy sauce; check cereal label
recipes.note: Photo illustrates a similar dish; appearance and ingredients may differ. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Only fully dry, crisp clusters may be stored in an airtight container at room temperature, for up to 3 days. Refrigerate any softened or damp batch.

recipes.title: Coconut Tamarind Fish Curry

ingredients.name: Firm white fish fillets (e.g., cod or snapper), 3cm cubes

steps: Cook the rice and measured rice water according to package directions. Heat oil in a large deep pan over medium-high heat. Add mustard seeds and wait for them to pop, then add curry leaves and onions.
Sauté onions for 7 minutes until golden, then stir in ginger, garlic, turmeric, and chili powder; cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Whisk tamarind paste with water and add to the pan along with the coconut milk and salt. Bring to a gentle simmer.
Add fish pieces carefully into the sauce. Do not stir vigorously as this will break the fish.
Simmer covered for 8-10 minutes. Check that the fish reaches 145°F / 63°C and flakes easily with a fork.
Fold spinach into the curry for 2 minutes to wilt it, then remove from heat once fish reaches 145°F / 63°C.
Divide cooked rice into six bowls and spoon equal portions of fish, spinach and curry sauce over each.
Serve hot immediately. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, use within 3 days, and reheat to 165°F / 74°C.
recipes.note: Serve with steamed basmati rice. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days.

recipes.title: Spiced Peanut Sundal
steps: Heat oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Add mustard seeds and wait until they pop.
Add urad dal and fry for 1 minute until golden brown, then add curry leaves, green chili, and asafoetida.
Add the roasted peanuts to the skillet and toss well to coat them in the tempered spices.
Cook for 3-4 minutes on low heat to ensure the peanuts are warm and aromatic.
Stir in the grated coconut and salt, tossing for another 1 minute.
Remove from heat and let sit for 2 minutes to allow the flavors to meld.
Divide into six small bowls for serving.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, use within 2 days, and reheat cooked leftovers to 165°F / 74°C.
recipes.allergens: Peanuts, mustard; asafoetida blends may contain wheat
recipes.note: A traditional South Indian protein-rich snack. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours because this snack contains fresh coconut; use within 2 days.

recipes.title: Roasted Root Vegetable and Lentil Medley
steps: Preheat the oven to 400°F / 200°C. Toss parsnips, carrots, and beets with 30mL oil, salt, and pepper on two large baking sheets.
Roast for 35-40 minutes, turning halfway through, until the vegetables are tender and caramelized at the edges.
While vegetables roast, place lentils and broth in a pot. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 25-30 minutes until tender but not mushy.
Drain any excess broth from the lentils and transfer them to a large mixing bowl.
Whisk the remaining 15mL oil with balsamic vinegar and thyme; pour over the warm lentils.
Fold the roasted vegetables into the lentils gently.
Divide into six plates and top with chopped walnuts.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, use within 4 days, and reheat to 165°F / 74°C.
recipes.note: A hearty autumn dish focusing on root vegetables. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 4 days.

recipes.title: Spiced Pear and Oat Crumble Pots
steps: Preheat the oven to 375°F / 190°C. Toss diced pears with lemon juice, vanilla, and 15mL maple syrup in a bowl.
Divide the pear mixture among six small oven-safe ramekins.
In a separate bowl, combine oats, almond flour, and cinnamon. Rub in the chilled butter with your fingers until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs.
Stir in the remaining maple syrup into the crumble topping.
Sprinkle the topping evenly over the pears in each ramekin.
Bake for 20-25 minutes until the fruit is bubbling and the topping is golden brown.
Remove from the oven and let cool for 5 minutes before serving.
Store leftovers in the refrigerator for up to 3 days; reheat in the oven or microwave.
recipes.note: Perfect for a crisp October evening. Developed for Real Family. Not kitchen-tested. Photo illustrates a similar dish.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days.
